q: The electronic component that lets current pass easily in one direction only, and is therefore used to convert AC into DC, is the:
x: A diode conducts when forward biased and blocks current when reverse biased, so it passes only one direction of current. Capacitors, resistors and inductors do not act as one-way valves.

q: In a half-wave rectifier with an ideal diode, what is the voltage across the load resistor during the half-cycle in which the diode is reverse biased?
o: Equal to the peak input voltage
Equal to the peak input voltage but reversed
x: A reverse-biased ideal diode is an open circuit, so no current flows through the load and the voltage across it is zero for that half-cycle.

q: A full-wave rectifier is built from a centre-tapped transformer and two diodes. At any moment while the load carries current, how many of these diodes are conducting?
o: It alternates between none and two
x: In the centre-tapped circuit the two diodes take turns: one conducts during the positive half-cycle and the other during the negative half-cycle, so only one conducts at a time.

q: To smooth the pulsating output of a rectifier, a component is connected in parallel with the load resistor. This component is a:
x: A capacitor charges during each pulse and discharges through the load between pulses, filling in the gaps and reducing the ripple.

q: A half-wave rectifier uses a silicon diode that drops 0.7 V when conducting. If the peak AC input is 12.7 V, the peak voltage across the load is:
x: The diode takes 0.7 V of the forward voltage, so the load receives 12.7 − 0.7 = 12 V at the peak. Adding the drop (13.4 V) or halving the input are common mistakes.

q: An advantage of a bridge rectifier over the two-diode full-wave rectifier is that the bridge circuit:
o: Produces pure DC without any filter
Does not need a centre-tapped transformer
x: The bridge uses four diodes but works with an ordinary transformer secondary, whereas the two-diode circuit needs a centre tap. Its output is still pulsating DC without a filter.

q: A diode can be used for rectification because it has:
o: High resistance in forward bias and low resistance in reverse bias
Low resistance in forward bias and very high resistance in reverse bias
The same low resistance in both directions
The same high resistance in both directions
x: Rectification needs a one-way device. A diode conducts easily in forward bias but almost blocks current in reverse bias.

q: A full-wave rectifier works from 50 Hz mains. What is the time interval between the starts of successive output pulses?
x: Full-wave output has 2 × 50 = 100 pulses per second, so one pulse every 1/100 s = 10 ms. 20 ms would be the half-wave value.

q: In a working half-wave rectifier, the diode is taken out and put back the other way round. The output across the load now:
o: Is still half-wave DC, but of opposite polarity, using the other half-cycle
Becomes zero for the whole cycle
x: The reversed diode conducts during the other half of the input cycle, so the load still gets one pulse per cycle but with the current in the opposite direction.

q: Pure silicon is doped with a pentavalent impurity such as arsenic. The majority charge carriers in the resulting material are:
x: Each pentavalent atom has one spare valence electron, giving n-type material in which free electrons are the majority carriers.

q: A trivalent impurity atom such as boron, added to silicon to make p-type material, is called:
x: A trivalent atom leaves a vacancy (hole) in a covalent bond that can accept an electron, so it is called an acceptor. Pentavalent atoms are donors.

q: The large current through a forward-biased PN junction is carried mainly by:
o: Immobile ions in the depletion region
x: Forward bias lowers the barrier so holes from the p-side and electrons from the n-side (majority carriers) cross in large numbers. Minority carriers give the tiny reverse current.

q: In an unbiased PN junction, the electric field across the depletion region points:
o: From the n-side to the p-side
From the p-side to the n-side
Along the junction, parallel to it
Nowhere, because the field is zero
x: The n-side of the depletion region holds positive ions and the p-side holds negative ions, so the field points from the positive n-side towards the negative p-side.

q: A diode made from germanium begins to conduct appreciably once the forward voltage across it exceeds roughly:
x: The barrier potential of a germanium junction is about 0.3 V; 0.7 V is the value for silicon.

q: A 4.7 V battery, a 1 kΩ resistor and a silicon diode are connected in series, with the n-side of the diode joined to the positive terminal of the battery. The current is approximately:
x: With the n-side at the positive terminal the diode is reverse biased, so only a negligible current flows. 4 mA would be the answer if it were forward biased: (4.7 − 0.7)/1000.

q: A hole in a p-type semiconductor is best described as:
o: A free proton that moves through the crystal
A negative ion fixed in the crystal lattice
An extra electron supplied by the impurity atom
A vacancy left where an electron is missing from a covalent bond, acting as a positive charge
x: A hole is a missing electron in a bond. Neighbouring electrons can move into it, so the hole moves and behaves like a positive carrier; it is not a proton.

q: When a PN junction is connected in forward bias, the holes in the p-region and the free electrons in the n-region are pushed:
x: The positive terminal repels holes and the negative terminal repels electrons, driving both towards the junction, where they cross and recombine.

q: A forward-biased silicon diode (drop 0.7 V) is in series with a resistor R across a 3.7 V battery. The current is 6 mA. What is R?
x: Voltage across R = 3.7 − 0.7 = 3.0 V, so R = 3.0/0.006 = 500 Ω. Ignoring the diode drop gives 617 Ω.
